facts.claim: UNESCO page title 'Indonesian Batik' (state: Indonesia), inscribed in 2009 (4.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Page live, HTTP 200.

UNESCO's own description says special varieties of batik are incorporated into celebrations of marriage and pregnancy, and that batik runs through life from infancy (batik baby slings) to death (funerary batik). The element is tagged 'Wedding' among its keywords. So UNESCO's text DOES link batik to weddings and life-cycle ceremonies.
UNESCO describes the method: designs drawn on cotton or silk with dots and lines of hot wax, which resists dye; the craft is often handed down within families for generations.

UNESCO page title 'Kebaya: knowledge, skills, traditions and practices', a joint (multinational) element of Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, inscribed in 2024 (19.COM) on the Representative List. Page live, HTTP 200. Found via the UNESCO lists search for 'kebaya'.

UNESCO's kebaya text says it is worn at casual and formal events, social gatherings and festivals, and in performing arts. It does NOT mention weddings or life-cycle ceremonies, and 'Wedding' is not among its keyword tags. The article must not say UNESCO links kebaya to weddings.

UNESCO describes kebaya as a front-opening top, often embroidered, fastened with brooches or buttons, made in various lengths and wearable with a matching sarong; making skills were traditionally passed informally from mothers to daughters.

Kraton Yogyakarta (official palace site, 'Dhaup Ageng', dated 16 April 2017): in Javanese tradition the wedding is hosted by the bride's side. Context: this page describes the royal wedding of a Sultan's daughter, simplified over time.

Kraton Yogyakarta: siraman is the ritual bathing of both bride and groom-to-be, meant to cleanse or purify them outwardly and inwardly; it is performed by the mother, the future mother-in-law and senior relatives of the bride-to-be as a form of blessing; bride and groom are bathed at separate times and places, the bride first.
Kraton Yogyakarta (royal practice): the bride-to-be is bathed with water drawn from seven springs mixed with flowers. Royal palace context; do not present the seven springs as universal.

Kraton Yogyakarta: after siraman the couple are dressed and made up; for the bride this usually means shaving the fine hairs on the forehead and nape to form the outline (cengkorongan) of the paes ageng makeup. Source supports ngerik in substance (the verb used is 'mengerik'); the term 'juru paes' is not on the page.

Kraton Yogyakarta: midodareni takes place on the night before the core wedding rites; the name comes from 'bidadari' (heavenly nymph), expressing the hope that the bride will look as beautiful as a nymph; nymphs are believed to descend near midnight; the custom is linked to the Jaka Tarub and Nawangsih story.

Kraton Yogyakarta: the akad nikah is the core rite that makes the couple husband and wife; the ijab qobul vow is spoken; in the royal version it takes place in the palace mosque (Masjid Panepen), is attended by men, and the Sultan himself marries off his daughter. Royal context only.

Kraton Yogyakarta: panggih is the meeting of bride and groom after they are legally married; they take turns throwing rolled betel leaves (gantal), the groom first; the bride then washes the groom's feet and an egg is broken. The royal version adds pondongan (carrying the bride). The page lists gantal before foot-washing and egg; it does not name the sindur cloth walk.
facts.conflicts: Royal version: groom 4 gantal, bride 3 gantal. Counts may differ in non-royal practice; do not state counts as universal.

facts.claim: Kraton Yogyakarta: after panggih come tampa kaya (groom pours coins and grains for the bride, symbolising his duty to provide) and dhahar klimah (shared meal in which the groom forms rice into three portions for the bride).

Kraton Yogyakarta ('Upacara Daur Hidup Masyarakat Jawa', 7 August 2017, citing a 2009 Yogyakarta provincial culture office book): marriage is one of the three key life phases with birth and death; Javanese marriage has three stages: pre-wedding, wedding and post-wedding.

Widyaparwa 49(1) 2021 (peer-reviewed, published by Balai Bahasa DIY under the Indonesian education ministry), Nardilla: studies panyandra, the poetic narration by the master of ceremonies during the panggih ceremony in the Surakarta style (Nganjuk, East Java), finding similes and metaphors of beauty, splendour and good wishes for the couple's household.

Official copy (BPK legal database) of Presidential Instruction No. 1 of 1991 on disseminating the Kompilasi Hukum Islam: KHI Book I covers marriage law; issued 10 June 1991; the Minister of Religious Affairs is instructed to disseminate it for use by government agencies and the public. The downloadable PDF is the 2-page instruction only, not the KHI annex text, so the specific akad requirements (wali, two witnesses, ijab kabul, mahar) were NOT confirmed from an official copy in this run.

insider_details.detail: Siraman and midodareni both fall before the core rites, so a couple planning a Javanese-style destination weekend should treat them as separate events with their own timing, family roles and outfit changes, not as add-ons on the wedding day.

Siraman is led by mothers and senior women of the bride's family, so travelling elders need to arrive in time for the day before the ceremony; build their flights and rooms around that, not around the reception.

Traditional bridal paes makeup starts right after siraman with shaping of the hairline, so hair and makeup scheduling needs a long, unhurried block, and photographers should know which moments the family wants captured.

Batik suits wedding-week dressing on solid ground: UNESCO's own listing ties special batik to celebrations of marriage. Kebaya is UNESCO-listed too, but its listing speaks of formal events and festivals rather than weddings, so describe kebaya as formal dress worn by many brides rather than citing UNESCO for the wedding link.

Panggih is full of small symbolic steps (betel-leaf throw, foot-washing, egg) narrated by a master of ceremonies, so brief non-Indonesian guests beforehand, for example in the order of service, so they can follow what is happening.
